"Ma, everyone's going to see me in the class photo with this haircut. My life is over."
Dolma put down the ladle. "It's shorter than you wanted."
"It's a disaster. Nobody has ever looked this stupid."
"That sounds really miserable, Anirban. Sit. Tell me."
He talked for ten minutes about the photo, the class group chat, and Riddhi's cousin, who would definitely laugh. Dolma listened, nodding.
"Can I tell you something?" she said at last. "At fifteen I cut my own fringe with kitchen scissors before my aunt's wedding."
"Seriously?"
"Seriously. Your cousin Pema has the photo."
Anirban almost smiled. "Is it bad?"
"Terrible. And the wedding was still lovely."

qa.q: What did Dolma do before her aunt's wedding when she was fifteen?
qa.a: She cut her own fringe with kitchen scissors.

qa.q: Why does the haircut feel like the end of Anirban's life?
qa.a: Anirban feels embarrassed and panicked, as though everyone will be looking at him, so a short haircut seems like something the whole class will notice and remember.

qa.q: Which of Dolma's choices let Anirban almost smile?
qa.a: Listening for ten minutes first, then sharing her own fringe story, so he could see his worry from a wider view without being dismissed.

qa.q: How does Dolma seem to see Anirban's panic?
qa.a: Dolma treats it as real to him rather than silly, while quietly knowing it will pass, just as her own fringe disaster did.

grounding: A mother listens to her teenage son's haircut panic without dismissing it and gently widens his view with her own story.

passage:
Last term, Yusuf in my Class 10 English section handed in an essay that began, "No one in history has felt as trapped as I do." My first thought was to circle "history" in red. I'm glad I didn't.
Instead I wrote in the margin, "I believe you feel trapped. Tell me more?" He came to the staffroom the next day and talked about exam pressure and an older brother everyone compares him to. I mostly listened.
Over the next few weeks I gave him things to read: a letter by a sixteen-year-old in old Kolkata, a poem by a young mill worker. In March he wrote, "Maybe lots of people felt trapped. They still wrote."
I kept that essay.
— Ms Reena

qa.q: How did Yusuf's essay begin?
qa.a: "No one in history has felt as trapped as I do."

qa.q: Why did Ms Reena decide not to circle 'history' in red?
qa.a: Ms Reena seems to have realised that correcting the exaggeration would dismiss a feeling that was real to Yusuf, and he might stop sharing.

qa.q: What did Ms Reena choose to do over the following weeks, and how did it help?
qa.a: Ms Reena gave Yusuf writing by other young people who felt trapped, so he could widen his own view instead of being told he was wrong.

qa.q: What might the staffroom talk have meant to Yusuf?
qa.a: It was likely a rare chance to be listened to about the pressure and the comparisons with his brother, without being judged.

grounding: A teacher looks back on treating a teenager's 'no one in history' feeling as real while slowly widening his view through reading.

passage:
Coach's notes, U-16 football
12 October: Lalit (15) missed an open goal and walked off saying, "The whole school will be laughing at me on Monday." His father was about to tell him not to be dramatic; I asked for a word first. I didn't tell Lalit it was nothing. I said, "That miss really stung." He nodded, eyes down.
Plan for the next few weeks: pair him with Irfan, a Class 12 striker, for shooting drills. Irfan misses too and laughs about it. After each match, ask Lalit what he thinks others noticed, then compare.
9 November: Missed again today. Shrugged. "Happens to everyone," he said.
— Chaitanya

qa.q: Who did Chaitanya pair Lalit with for shooting drills?
qa.a: Irfan, a Class 12 striker.

qa.q: Why did Lalit believe the whole school would be laughing on Monday?
qa.a: Lalit felt ashamed and stung, because one mistake felt as if everyone saw it and would remember it, so the miss seemed far bigger to Lalit than to anyone else.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya choose to do instead of letting Lalit be called dramatic?
qa.a: Chaitanya named the sting first, then planned drills with Irfan and after-match check-ins to widen Lalit's view slowly over weeks.

qa.q: How might Lalit's father see the coach stepping in?
qa.a: He may have felt a little sidelined at first, but could also see that listening worked better than telling Lalit not to be dramatic.

grounding: A coach's notes show a teen's 'everyone will laugh' feeling taken seriously and gently widened over several weeks.

passage:
Friday night
Tanuja came home and slammed her bag down. A pimple, the day before the dance. "Everyone will stare at it the whole time. Nobody has ever had one this bad, Amma. You don't understand." My first thought was, nobody is looking at your chin, beta. I bit it back. Fifteen is like this; I remember it. I just said, "That sounds really stressful." She talked for twenty minutes, and I mostly listened.
Later, over dinner, I asked what Riya was nervous about. She paused. "Riya's scared she'll forget the steps. She practised all week." A little silence. "Hm. I didn't even ask her." Small step, but a real one. I'll keep asking about others, slowly, without lecturing. She took the concealer to school and a cup of chai to her room. Good enough.
— Nikita

qa.q: What was Riya scared about before the dance?
qa.a: That she would forget the steps.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel like saying, and why did she hold it back?
qa.a: Nikita felt a little impatient and wanted to say nobody would look at Tanuja's chin, but held back because she saw this self-focus as normal at fifteen and wanted Tanuja to feel heard.

qa.q: Which of Nikita's choices gently widened Tanuja's view?
qa.a: Asking at dinner what Riya was nervous about, which led Tanuja to notice she hadn't asked her friend.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt when her mother simply said it sounded stressful?
qa.a: Tanuja likely felt listened to rather than dismissed, which is why she kept talking for twenty minutes.

grounding: A mother's diary shows her treating her teen daughter's self-focus as a normal stage, listening first and slowly widening her view.

passage: Salma, who taught English at the village school near Hassan, noticed Uday at the back again with his feet tucked under the bench. His shoes had split at the toes. "Everyone laughs at me, Ma'am," he said after class. "No one has ever been as poor as me." Salma could see that nobody was laughing. Most of the class wore old slippers. But she didn't say that. She listened. "That sounds like it makes every day hard." He nodded. Over the next weeks she gave him small jobs: handing out books, reading at the front. She paired him with Raju, who also had patched shoes. By the end of term Uday laughed at Raju's jokes, and forgot to hide his feet.

qa.q: What had happened to Uday's shoes?
qa.a: They had split at the toes.

qa.q: Why did Salma choose to listen instead of telling Uday nobody was laughing?
qa.a: Salma felt patient and caring, understanding that his self-focus was a normal stage and that dismissing it would only make him feel unheard.

qa.q: How did Salma widen Uday's view over time?
qa.a: She gave him small jobs at the front and paired him with Raju, so he could see others shared his situation and he wasn't being watched.

qa.q: How might Uday see the class by the end of term?
qa.a: He probably sees classmates as friends rather than judges, laughing with Raju and forgetting his shoes.

grounding: Shows a teacher recognising a teenager's self-focus as a normal stage, listening without dismissing, and gently widening his view over time.

passage: In their small São Paulo apartment, Priscila heard the bedroom door slam. Her daughter Nadia, sixteen, had got a bad mark in physics. "My life is over," Nadia shouted. "Everyone will know. You don't understand. Nobody has ever failed like this." Priscila felt the old urge to say, I failed physics twice, it's nothing. She held it back. She sat on the edge of the bed. "That sounds awful. Tell me." Nadia talked for twenty minutes. Priscila mostly nodded. The next week, at dinner, she mentioned casually that Nadia's cousin had once failed chemistry and now taught it. Nadia rolled her eyes. But a month later, she said, "Maybe people forget about marks faster than I thought."

qa.q: How long did Nadia talk after Priscila sat on the bed?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Priscila hold back from saying she had failed physics twice?
qa.a: Priscila felt the urge to comfort with her own story but was cautious, sensing it might feel dismissive while Nadia was upset.

qa.q: What approach helped widen Nadia's view, and why did it work?
qa.a: Listening first, then a week later casually mentioning a cousin's story, let Nadia hear it without feeling corrected.

qa.q: How might Nadia see her bad mark a month later?
qa.a: Nadia seems calmer, starting to see that others don't remember marks as much as she feared.

grounding: Shows a parent recognising a teenager's self-focus as normal, listening without dismissing, and widening the view over time.

passage: In the girls' hostel of the Jaipur school, the warden, Zainab, found Nirmala, fifteen, curled on her bed on a Sunday. "They're all talking about me," Nirmala said. "Because I cried in the dining hall. Nobody has ever been so homesick." Zainab had seen this almost every year. She didn't say so. She sat with her. "Being far from home is really hard. Tell me what you miss." Nirmala talked about her grandmother's garden. Zainab listened. The following Sunday, Zainab invited three girls to help her plant marigolds by the gate, Nirmala among them. While they dug, one girl said she had cried every night for a month in her first term. Nirmala stared. "You?" Zainab kept her eyes on the soil and smiled.

qa.q: What did Zainab invite the girls to plant?
qa.a: Marigolds by the gate.

qa.q: Why did Zainab not tell Nirmala that this happened almost every year?
qa.a: Zainab felt compassion and understood that pointing out how common it was might make Nirmala feel dismissed, so she listened first.

qa.q: How did the marigold planting widen Nirmala's view?
qa.a: It brought her together with other girls, one of whom shared her own homesickness, so Nirmala could learn she wasn't the only one.

qa.q: How might the girl who admitted crying every night feel after sharing?
qa.a: She might feel a bit exposed but also glad, seeing that her story helped Nirmala feel less alone.

grounding: Shows a hostel warden treating a teenager's self-focus as a normal stage, listening kindly, and gently widening her view over time.

passage:
Dear Aparna,

Last night you said, "You don't understand anything, Papa. Nobody feels the way I do." I didn't argue. I want you to know I was listening.

I remember being fifteen, beti. I felt the same: that my feelings were bigger and more unique than anyone's. It's a normal part of growing up, and your feelings are real.

I won't tell you they're small. But I'd like to share, slowly, some of what I felt at your age, if you'll let me. Maybe you'll find we're not so different.

Whenever you want to talk, my door is open.

Your Papa,
Vijay

qa.q: What did Aparna say to Papa last night?
qa.a: "You don't understand anything, Papa. Nobody feels the way I do."

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when Aparna said he didn't understand?
qa.a: Vijay felt patient and caring, choosing to listen instead of arguing because he remembered feeling the same.

qa.q: What does Vijay's letter do well?
qa.a: It accepts Aparna's feelings as real, avoids dismissing them, and gently offers to share his own past to widen her view over time.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Aparna might feel surprised and a little softer, feeling heard instead of judged.

grounding: A father recognises his teenager's self-focus as normal, listens without dismissing, and gently offers to widen her view.

passage:
I'm Manoj, and I've taught class nine for ten years. Every year there's a student like Alka. Last month she told me, "Sir, no one in history has had a week as bad as mine."

A younger me would have laughed or said, "Grow up." Now I know it's a stage. At that age, it genuinely feels like you're the only one.

So I said, "Tell me about it." She did: a fight with her best friend, a bad test, a missed bus. I listened. Then I said, "That does sound like a hard week."

A few days later, I lent her a novel about a girl with a terrible week. She came back and said, "She's just like me!" That's how the view widens: slowly, with company.

qa.q: What did Manoj lend Alka?
qa.a: A novel about a girl with a terrible week.

qa.q: How does Manoj feel about students like Alka now?
qa.a: He feels calm, patient and understanding, seeing their self-focus as a normal stage rather than something to mock.

qa.q: What did Manoj do that helped Alka widen her view?
qa.a: He listened, agreed it was a hard week, and later lent her a novel about someone like her.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt when Manoj listened to her?
qa.a: Alka probably felt heard and less alone.

grounding: A teacher sees a teenager's self-focus as a normal stage, listens without dismissing, and gently widens her view over time.

passage:
I'm Bhupen, Wasim's uncle. He's sixteen and lives with us this year while his parents are abroad.

Some days he shuts himself in his room and says, "Nobody gets it. Everyone's staring at me at school." His aunt wanted to tell him he's overreacting. I asked her to wait.

I don't know exactly what's in his head. But I remember that age. So I just sit with him, sometimes in silence. Once I told him about how, at sixteen, I thought my voice cracking was the end of the world.

He laughed a little. Last week he came out and asked if I wanted to watch cricket. He talked about a boy in his class who feels the same way. That felt like progress.

qa.q: How old is Wasim?
qa.a: He's sixteen.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel when Wasim shuts himself away?
qa.a: Bhupen feels calm, patient and a little worried, remembering being sixteen himself.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that helped Wasim?
qa.a: He sat with Wasim, shared his own teenage worry, and didn't tell him he was overreacting.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel noticing a classmate feels the same way?
qa.a: Wasim probably feels less alone and relieved that he isn't the only one.

grounding: An uncle recognises a teenager's self-focus as normal, listens without dismissing, and gently widens his view.

passage:
Monday: Rekha comes home from school and announces that her life is "literally the worst in the world" because she wore the wrong shoes for the class photo. Her mother, Zeenat, bites back "some children have no shoes" and listens instead. "That sounds so embarrassing."
Thursday: Rekha is still talking about the shoes. Zeenat asks, "Did anyone else have a photo problem?" Rekha thinks. "Actually, the girl next to me blinked." "How did she feel?" "Terrible, I think."
The next Sunday: Looking at the printed class photo together, Rekha laughs. "You can't even see my shoes. And her blink is kind of cute." Zeenat smiles and says nothing, pleased.

qa.q: What went wrong in the class photo, according to Rekha?
qa.a: She wore the wrong shoes.

qa.q: What might Zeenat be feeling when she bites back her comment?
qa.a: She is probably tempted to feel impatient, but chooses patience and empathy, seeing this self-focus as a normal stage.

qa.q: How did Zeenat widen Rekha's view over time?
qa.a: She first listened and agreed it sounded embarrassing, then asked whether anyone else had a photo problem, letting Rekha notice another girl's feelings.

qa.q: How does Rekha feel about the photo by Sunday?
qa.a: She feels lighter and amused, seeing that her shoes don't show and even finding the other girl's blink cute.

grounding: A mother treats her teenager's self-focus as a normal stage, listens without dismissing, and gently widens her view over a week.

passage: Avni, you're new to teaching teenagers, so here's something from when my son Jugraj was fifteen. Every evening he said nobody at school had ever suffered like him, and that everyone laughed when he walked in. My first instinct was to say, "Stop the drama, nobody's looking at you." Your Gurpreet aunty bit her tongue, thank God. I just listened. After a few weeks, I asked whether his friend Manpreet ever felt left out. He thought for a long time. "Yes, actually. At lunch." Slowly, month by month, he started noticing others. By seventeen he was the one sitting with the new boy. Patience, beta. The world gets bigger for them if we don't slam the door.

qa.q: Who did Jugraj sit with by seventeen?
qa.a: The new boy.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet's first instinct, and what did she feel?
qa.a: To say "Stop the drama"; she likely felt impatient and frustrated, but chose to listen instead.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Biting her tongue and listening, then later asking about his friend's feelings, which widened his view gradually.

qa.q: How might Jugraj have felt if she had said "Stop the drama"?
qa.a: Dismissed and more alone, probably shutting down instead of slowly noticing others.

grounding: An elder recalls treating her teenage son's self-focus as a normal stage, listening and slowly widening his view.

passage: It was the day before the annual exams, the staff room was chaos, and Siddharth sir had forty papers to check. Then Pallavi appeared at the door, eyes red. "I can't read the news at assembly tomorrow. Everyone will stare at me. Nobody has ever been this nervous." Siddharth felt the urge to say, "Not now, Pallavi." Instead he pushed the papers aside. "That sounds really hard. Sit." He listened for five minutes. Then he asked, "Remember who read the news last week?" "The boy from 9C." "How was he?" "His voice shook the whole time." "Did you laugh?" "No. I felt bad for him." Pallavi paused. "Oh." The next day she read, her voice shaking a little, and nobody laughed.

qa.q: What did Pallavi say she couldn't do tomorrow?
qa.a: Read the news at assembly.

qa.q: What did Siddharth feel when Pallavi appeared?
qa.a: He felt the urge to say "Not now", stressed with forty papers, but chose patience.

qa.q: How did Siddharth widen Pallavi's view?
qa.a: He listened first, then asked about last week's reader and how she felt about his shaky voice, letting her see that others weren't judging her.

qa.q: How does Pallavi's view change?
qa.a: She realises she felt sympathy, not scorn, for the last reader, so others will probably feel the same about her.

grounding: A teacher treats a teenager's sense that everyone is watching as normal, listens despite pressure, and gently widens her view.

passage: Nitin came home from tuition, dropped his bag in the doorway of the Pune flat and announced, "My life is literally over. I wore the wrong shoes to the farewell and everyone will remember it forever." Sudha, his mother, was chopping onions and felt the old urge to say, "Nobody cares about your shoes." Then she remembered crying over a bad haircut at his age. Instead she said, "That sounds awful to walk in with." Nitin sat down and talked for twenty minutes. A week later, over tea, Sudha asked what his friend Arvind had worn. Nitin paused. "Actually, Arvind's trousers were torn. No one said anything." He looked at her, half embarrassed, half amused. Sudha only smiled and passed the biscuits.

qa.q: What did Nitin say had gone wrong at the farewell?
qa.a: He said he wore the wrong shoes to the farewell.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she held back "Nobody cares about your shoes"?
qa.a: She felt tempted and a little impatient, but remembering her own teenage upset made her sympathetic, so she chose to listen instead.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Listening first and asking about Arvind a week later worked, because Nitin felt taken seriously and then noticed by himself that others have awkward moments too.

qa.q: How does Nitin see the shoe problem once Sudha has listened?
qa.a: At first it feels huge and permanent to him; a week later he sees that Arvind's torn trousers went unnoticed and feels half embarrassed about his worry.

grounding: A parent treats her teenager's self-focus as a normal stage, listens without dismissing it, and later gently widens his view.
